How AI agents behave: lessons from 63M MCP tool callsProductsPricingDocsCommunityCompanyMoreGet started – free

BlogCopy page
How AI agents behave: lessons from 63M MCP tool calls
Natalia Amorim
Sep 30, 2026
Studies
(in my best David Attenborough voice): And here, in its natural habitat, we observe a new species of user emerging. It has no face and needs no mouse, it does not doomscroll or rage-click. Instead, the AI agent approaches quietly through an MCP server, reaching into the product to forage for data on behalf of its human. 
We're not describing a particularly mature ecosystem, but rather one that's being born, in real time, on our doorsteps. 
And so, like any responsible naturalists, we began observing it (by which we mean digging through our data to see what these agents are up to).
In the 90 days up to to September 16, agents made 63 million tool calls to PostHog's MCP, coming from 130,000 people.1 (For the latest numbers, check our live MCP leaderboard.)

Half of all agent traffic is Anthropic

First, a caveat: when we first looked into the data, almost half of it traffic was us. PostHog Desktop, the CLI, the Slack app, and our Signals scouts all reach the same MCP server as everyone else, and the scouts in particular never sleep. So for this section we've set our own agents aside and looked only at the 55% that comes from people using their own tools.2
In this timeframe, Claude Code was the biggest caller, making up 32% of third-party calls. OpenAI's Codex was second at 22%, then Cursor at 10%, Cowork at 7%, and a long tail of Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, ChatGPT, and Claude's Agent SDK at 2–3% each.
Roll it up by vendor and it's simpler: Anthropic surfaces make up about 50% of all third-party calls, OpenAI 25%, Cursor 10%, and everyone else fights over what's left.

About 14% of calls come from clients we can't place at all: homegrown scripts, unnamed bots, and agents that don't introduce themselves (rude).
Include our own agents and the picture inverts, by the way: our scouts run on Codex, which makes Codex 62% of all traffic. Just not a very interesting 62%.
The agent poking at your product almost certainly isn't in a chat window; it's in someone's code editor or terminal, running commands. Only about 7% of calls come from a chat window.

Agents ignore 95% of what we built
What do agents want? Turns out, not much (at least not in terms of variety). Sixty-three million calls, and it mostly comes down to two moves: running a SQL query (15.6 million calls – 25% of everything) and reading the schema to find out what's queryable in the first place (another 7%).
Between them, those two are 32% of all traffic. 

It's worth knowing there are three doors an agent can take to ask our MCP a data question:
It can write raw SQL. 
It can call one of our typed query wrappers – trends, funnels, retention – and skip the SQL entirely (3% of calls).
It can go through product analytics proper: creating, reading, and updating saved insights (another 3%). 
Agents overwhelmingly pick the first door. SQL gets about four times the traffic of the other two put together.

Reading the schema tells an agent what's in your data (which events you capture, what properties they carry). But another 4.5% of calls is the step before that: pulling up a skill, or searching the docs to work out how a particular tool wants to be called. 
So about 5% of calls are an agent looking something up rather than doing something.
A lot of our tools barely register, which is a little tragic, because PostHog's MCP has hundreds of different functionalities available. 
Give an agent a single prompt and it could spin up an A/B test today and ship the winning variant next week. It could open an error, read the stack trace, jump to the exact replay of the user who hit it, and patch the code. It could point an AI at a week of sessions and ask questions about it. The list goes on.

This is partly a note to self (we should advertise these better) and partly advice for anyone building an MCP: the good stuff needs to be discoverable.
If you want agents near the best parts of your product, you have to surface those tools legibly enough that a person remembers to point at them, but also so that an agent can find them without being told. 
Otherwise the best thing you built stays underwater, and nobody knows it's there.
Agents create 2.5x more insights than humans
In the last 30 days, agents created 252,000 insights through the MCP. People created 99,000 in the web app. 
Add PostHog AI on top and more than half of every insight made last month came from an AI of some kind.

It's the same story for dashboards, actions, and experiments: the MCP is the single biggest creation surface for all of them. 
Feature flags are the last product where humans still lead, and only by a few points.
Codex makes the fewest mistakes
Before anyone fights me: this measures how carefully each client forms its requests to our MCP, not how smart the agent is. A chattier, more exploratory agent will "error" more simply because it pokes at more things. 
That said, Codex is the standout: among third-party callers it errors on just 2% of calls. Cursor sits at 3.5%, Cowork at 5.3%, and Claude Code at 5.7%. Grouped by vendor, the gap holds: OpenAI clients error about 2% of the time, Anthropic clients about 5.5%.

The one thing we can't tell you yet is which model is most reliable. Agents can self-report their model to our MCP, but nothing verifies it, so we're not charting it until something does.
Here's a bit that made us sit up, though. Our own agents also run on Codex, against the same server, and they error just 1% of the time – half the rate of everyone else on the same model. The likeliest explanation is boring and useful: our prompts and tool descriptions were tuned against this exact MCP.

The more interesting question, though, isn't who errors, but what they get wrong. 
Agents almost never fail at finding data: reading the schema errors just 1.5% of the time, about 1 in 66. It's the querying that trips them up. The actual SQL call fails 4.4% of the time, nearly three times as often.

That said, agents don't panic: when one hits an error and the session keeps going, 39% of the time its very next move is to call the exact same tool again, and 75% of those retries work.

0.5% of calls cost 18% of the tokens
In the last 30 days our MCP handed agents 84 billion tokens, roughly thirty out for every one in.
A typical call is cheap: the median response is 440 tokens. But the tail is long; 5% of calls return more than 7,800 tokens, and 1% return more than 16,000.

And the tail isn't where you'd expect it. 
execute-sql is 23% of calls and 19% of tokens, which seems fair. But three dashboard tools (get, update, and reorder tiles) are 0.5% of calls and 18% of all tokens returned. 
A single 
dashboard-reorder-tiles call returns a median of 14,600 tokens, and at p95, 144,000. That's an entire context window just to move a tile.
You can't improve what you're not measuring
If your newest power user is a robot, you should probably know what it's doing; you can't improve an experience you're not measuring, and agents don't fill out NPS surveys.
So we launched a new analytics tool to help monitor MCP traffic. It was born from one of our internal hackathons, and was built to answer the questions we were asking ourselves.
It's called MCP analytics (currently in beta!) and it shows you who's calling, what they're calling, what's erroring and what isn't, how many calls each agent is making, what did they want that you don't have, and more. 
You can also step through any agent session tool call by tool call – the agent equivalent of a session replay – if you want to watch a robot think.
Want to see it at work? Our MCP leaderboard is MCP analytics running on our own server. It's built from the same data as this post, served through Endpoints.

Every number in this post came out of those views, pointed at our own server.
There's also no separate system to learn. Every call lands as a single 
$mcp_tool_call event on your normal events table, so the purpose-built views are there if you want them – and if you'd rather write SQL, build a dashboard, or point product analytics at it like any other event, that works too.
And it doesn't just watch. Your tool calls can serve as a signal source for Self-driving. A scout watches 
$mcp_tool_call telemetry for tools that need attention – high failure rates, agents retrying the same call, slow or bloated responses – weighs them by volume and reach, and files a report. If it's a server you own, that report can hand off to a coding agent that opens a pull request. 
Instrument MCP Analytics with one command
The wizard sets up the SDK and starts capturing tool calls.
npx @posthog/wizard mcp-analyticsLearn more
All figures are from PostHog's own MCP server (the 
$mcp_tool_call event), so read them as "what we see on one busy server," not a census of all MCP everywhere. Headline counts cover the 90 days to September 16, 2026, and include our own traffic: PostHog Desktop, CLI, Slack app, and Signals scouts account for about 45% of every call. The other 55% comes from roughly 126,000 people using their own agents. Per-tool error rates and retry behavior use the last 30 days. We deliberately used only tool names, categories, client names, and counts, not the free-text "intent" agents send, so nothing here contains user data.↩
Client breakdowns and per-client error rates use the last 14 days, exclude calls where PostHog's own surfaces identify themselves as the consumer, and use PostHog's resolved harness label rather than the raw client name the SDK reports – that raw property only rides the session's 
initialize handshake, so grouping on it directly buckets most calls as unknown. Reliable client identification only landed in August 2026, which is why the client window is shorter than the headline window. Error rate reflects how a client forms requests, not the agent's underlying quality.↩PostHog is your product's context layer. How AI changes the way PostHog is used - PostHogProductsPricingDocsCommunityCompanyMoreGet started – free

How AI changes the way PostHog is used
Ian Vanagas
Nov 19, 2026
AI
People can't stop talking about how AI changes the way products are used. We can't stop writing about it. 
And although theorizing is fun, hard numbers are better. Here's how AI has actually changed the way PostHog is being used based on the data we capture.
Note: Most of this data is a snapshot from September 2026, and a lot of it is new:
MCP Analytics was only released into alpha in June. 
The source of object creation (human vs AI) was set up at different times for different products.
Data from PostHog's own agents wasn't always separated. 
This can makes AI trends seem sharper than they actually are. 
AI creates a majority of dashboards and insights
We count creation creation through our MCP, CLI, installation wizard, Slack app, Scouts, and PostHog AI as "AI". By that definition, AI creates a huge share of objects across PostHog's most popular products: 
ObjectAIWeb UIAPI
Insights58.7%15.0%25.3%
Dashboards56.4%23.6%18.4%
Workflows47.4%33.2%19.5%
Experiments45.8%27.7%26.3%
Feature flags36.1%36.6%21.8%
The share of dashboards built with AI is roughly flat since April 2026 (up from 54%). Others have seen more recent and rapid adoption:
Insights is up from 43% to 59%
Experiments is up from 19.9% to 45.8%
Feature flags is up from 14.3% to 36.1%

The UI is not dead, even for agent users
Do people come back to what AI creates? To check, we counted an object as "viewed" if someone opened it at least a day after it was created, and within 30 days. The viewing gap between AI-created and UI-created objects is biggest for insights:
ProductAI created, UI viewedUI created and viewedStill viewed day 15–30 (AI / UI)
Insights7%24%2% / 9%
Dashboards52%54%28% / 30%
Experiments63%71%31% / 41%
Workflows34%47%14% / 19%
Just because someone uses agents, doesn't mean they give up on the UI either. 96% of agent-heavy users (meaning they made 200+ calls through their agent in September) still use the UI. 
People who start using agents kept the same number of days with a UI pageview (median of 9), while similar users who didn't start with agents fell from 8 to 5. 30% of experiments created through the MCP were later edited in the UI, and about of a third of their launches happened there too. 
Agents speak SQL
74% of MCP queries are SQL (as opposed to trend, funnel, or schema queries), while in the UI only 43% are. Overall, 
execute-sql is our most popular MCP tool at 52.3% of all tool calls. It's used 4x more than any other tool.

Interestingly, across people who use both, Claude calls 
execute-sql a lot more than Codex (66% to 38%). Codex relies more on schema lookups (21% to 8%), while Claude is willing to fail and try again. 
5.2% of Claude's SQL calls fail compared to only 3.6% of Codex's.

Agents and humans prefer different products
If you compare MCP tool calls with UI pageviews, you get a sense of what products are more used by one or the other. 
UI-dominant products include: replay (0.04 MCP tool calls per UI pageview), dashboards (0.06), web analytics (0.07), and surveys (0.07).
Agent-heavy products include logs (1.10), error tracking (0.61), insights (0.50), and warehouse/CDP (0.49).
Although this undercounts unassignable SQL tool calls, the split is clear: watching and browsing happens in the UI; investigating and debugging happen with AI.

The surface shapes the work
Cursor is a leader for error tracking usage. 5.8% of its calls are related to error tracking, compared to 2.9% of Codex's and 2.1% of Claude's.
OpenAI reads the docs. 
docs-search is 5.5% of Codex's calls, but only 0.7% of Claude Code's.

The wizard is for setup. 64% of its tool calls are for writing (creating or updating objects), much higher than the next largest write source (WebMCP at 22%).
Slack is almost the opposite: 78% is SQL and schema lookups, only 5% writes.
The PostHog team makes our 11x more Slack calls per user than our customers. Our team made 39% of all Slack app calls.
AI users adopt and use PostHog more
AI is drives adoption. Our AI installation wizard is the first way that happens. 14.2% of orgs who use it to install PostHog convert to paid against 2.6% for manual installs. They adopt an average 0.88 extra products in their second month against 0.36 for manual installs.

How I use skills for everything
Andy Maguire
Oct 20, 2026
Explainers, 
AI
When agent skills first came out, I thought they were silly. We are just casting magic spells now are we? Is that where we are?
But over time, I bought into the whole "context engineering" thing (as much as I fought the hype initially) and started using them more. Today, almost every interaction I have with an agent on any surface loads at least one skill from the PostHog skills store.
No really, my agent looked it up. Over the last 28 days, 78% of my 578 chats loaded a skill and 47% updated one (shoutout AI observability for making this easy as all my Claude Code sessions go there). 
I have about 139 skills in the store. About 100 of them are custom scouts, which are skills that run themselves on a schedule. The other 39 are for how I actually work, and those are what this post is about.
Jake gets it.
To be clear, this isn't a "try my magic skill bro" pitch. There's a little cottage industry of skills that promise to fix your agent, and I find it a bit cringe. I'm not taking a dependency on your skill, bro. Skills can turn into tech debt (agent debt?), so the bar for adopting someone else's should be very high.
What I'm evangelical about is the ways you use them.
Skills are magic context bombs
Most people think of skills as better prompts. Something that teaches the agent a trick. They aren't.
You should think of skills as little portable agentic memory systems. They are the perfect abstraction for tagging a bundle of context, so an agent (or I) can pull that context in exactly when it's needed and nowhere else. 
The body is typically a thin index. The bundled files hold the detail. The agent reads them and pulls only the files the current task touches. That's progressive disclosure, and it's mostly the point.
A lot of the time skills are used to provide the agent with instructions, but this will likely go away as models get better. They will just use their built in memory and tools to get what they need.
What won't go away is the need to manage context. This means telling agents what's true right now, what happened last session, what's in-flight, and what bit us before. That's the part I'm skills-pilled on, and the part that's changed my work the most. Here are some examples. 
1. Skills as a project tracker
Every meaningful piece of work I do is documented and maintained by my agents in one of two skills: 
self-driving-work and 
scouts-work (these are the two things I work on the most). 
They're siblings with identical conventions: a numbered 
issues/ backlog with an index, an 
ideas/ folder, 
open-prs.md, a rolling 14-day 
CHANGELOG.md, 
environment-notes.md for durable gotchas, and a 
HANDOVER.md that each session overwrites its own section of.
At the time I'm writing this, the 
self-driving-work skill is on version 433 with 126 bundled files, including 55 numbered issues, 17 ideas, and 39 pain points. I didn't write most of those. My agents did, at the end of sessions, because the skill tells them to.PostHog AI

self-driving-work v433, 126 bundled files├── SKILL.md the thin index├── HANDOVER.md one section per thread of work├── CHANGELOG.md rolling 14-day window├── environment-notes.md durable gotchas├── open-prs.md├── roadmap.md├── dogfooding.md├── field-feedback.md├── issues/ 55 issues + index│ ├── 01-reviewer-suggestion-regression.md│ ├── 02-crowd-fallback-provenance.md│ └── ...├── ideas/ 17 ideas + index│ ├── 01-rank-by-author-association.md│ └── ...├── pain-points/ 39 bad examples + index├── feedback/ 3 + index└── scripts/ └── task_summary_sampler.py
The loop looks like this:
I start a session on any surface (local Claude Code, a cloud task, Slack, PostHog AI, Codex) and say "let's check in on /phs self-driving work".
The agent uses my local 
/phs bridge skill, loads the remote skill, reads 
HANDOVER.md, scans the backlog index, and knows where we left off. We do the work in the repo and the product, not in the skill.
At the end of the session, the agent logs any new issue or idea, records any PR that opened or merged, adds one changelog line, and overwrites its handover section.
This is the lowest friction and most chill way I have ever found to deliver complex features over long horizons. The skill is the memory, and it's memory I get my agents to intentionally control and maintain.
I don't rely on a model's hidden memory feature that I can't read. The skill in PostHog shows exactly what my agents think is true. If it gets messy, I tell the agent to clean up, or better yet, it knows to follow certain protocols like trimming the changelog after 14 days (all skill edits are version tracked so it's recoverable if I need it).
I liked this pattern enough that I turned it into a template. 
project-template is in the community skills store. Install it once per area of work, bind the project name and the changelog window, and you have a living hub that any agent on your team can read and write.
My favorite part of the template is a small table the agent has to consult before writing anything down:
Still true in 30 days?Has an owner who refreshes it?Goes in
YesYes, a tracked work item
issues/NN or 
ideas/NN
YesNo, durable reference
environment-notes.md or a 
references/ file
No, but in flight nowYou, this sessionyour 
HANDOVER.md section
No, it just happenedNobody
CHANGELOG.md, one line
The table is there to stop the most common way these skills go wrong: the agent writes durable detail into the changelog, because the changelog is the file it was already editing. I watched that happen many times before I added the table.
You don't need all this structure on day one, though. For a new, messy project, just start a skill and tell your agent to keep its context there. Don't worry much about the layout. Agents do something sensible on their own, and in my experience, a skill only starts to get messy at around version 50. The important part is that the context is in a skill you can see, version, and load from anywhere.
2. Skills as a map of the stuff I work on
Filter our skills store to 
self-driving- and you get a map of how self-driving works inside PostHog: the alerts, the dashboards, the data warehouse layer, the Temporal workers, the debugging runbook, and the support rotation. Eleven skills, written by several people on the team. A new teammate, or a fresh agent session, can read that list and know where everything lives.
The most detailed part of the map is 
self-driving-dwh. It's the blueprint for the data warehouse views behind our internal self-driving analytics: an entity diagram of how scout runs, signals, reports, tasks, and PRs join, the keys that stitch them together, and a 
recipes/ folder of SQL that actually works.
The entity diagram in 
self-driving-dwh. Any agent that loads the skill gets the same picture I have in my head. Also, no one likes making ERDs but agents love it! (or have no choice)
When I say "use the /self-driving-dwh skill to help here", the agent knows how everything joins before it writes a query. The skill is on version 458, and I didn't write most of it. A scout, 
signals-scout-self-driving-dwh, checks that the views still sync, catches drift when a source table changes, and updates the skill when it fixes something. A skill maintained by a skill.
Another favorite example is 
self-driving-alerts. It's the single store for all 178 of our anomaly alerts: what each one watches, which dashboard tile it hangs off, which Slack channel it posts to, and why it exists. When we want a new alert, the agent reads the skill to see if we already have one, then adds the new one to the inventory as part of creating it.
Each skill is version tracked and we have an optional description string on all changes so you can easily see how the skill changed and by whom. Very useful for team level skills like this.
This also means we can compare any two versions of a skill body. Here, v61 against v73: the alert counts go up as new alerts get added. Remember, this is mostly text for agents to read. 
Stuff like this used to be really annoying to maintain somewhere – now you get it for practically free if you just put it in a skill and let your agents maintain it.
3. Skills as a runbook that learns
The alerts skill above records what exists. A runbook records what went wrong and how we fixed it, so it gets better every time something breaks.

self-driving-debugging is our runbook for when self-driving misbehaves in production and users have some issues we need to dig into.
The whole thing hangs off one line in the skill body: add or extend a reference every time we run down a new class of issue. When a support ticket turns into a real investigation, the agent writes what it found as a dated file in 
investigations/, then extends the matching reference so the next agent doesn't start from zero. Seven investigations in, it covers duplicate reports, competing PRs for one fix, oversold report titles, unaddressed review comments, and a data import source that emitted nothing.
Its sibling, 
scouts-debugging, does the same job for the scout fleet. Between them, "debug self-driving for team N" is a sentence I can say to an agent on any surface and get a real answer.
4. Skills as a daily driver
The 
andy-inbox skill is how I start most days. It pulls every report in the self-driving inbox where I'm a suggested reviewer, maps each one to its GitHub PR and issues, and renders one plain line per report: priority, age, review state, CI, and one next action.PostHog AI

In flight with a PR, newest report first
# Next Report PR Signals1 ENQUEUE (YOUR GO) fix(signals): give the revenue scout a supp… #108959 stamp✓ CI✓2 FIX CI fix(mcp): paginate large GitHub repository… #108947 stamp✓ CI2✗3 ENQUEUE (YOUR GO) fix(mcp): document the usable --json flag p… #108934 stamp✓ CI✓4 ENQUEUE (YOUR GO) fix(hogql): system schema discovery relapse␀… #108866 stamp✓ CI✓5 FIX CI fix(inbox): show why follow-up checks failed… #108829 stamp? The skill bundles Python scripts to do the boring parts: 
render_table.py builds the table from the API and 
gh, 
pr_candidates.py ranks reports that are ready for a Create PR press, 
merge_intent.py finds PRs I've approved that need agent work to get merged, and 
draft_task.py writes the payload to launch a PostHog task for a stalled row. So "get these three PRs green on CI" turns into three async tasks I can check on later.
It also has a 
working-set.md that records only what I've personally chosen to own, with four rules to guide it:
Check the live state first, the file second.
The API is the truth.
The file is a list of my commitments.
Never report status from the file alone.
There's a whole family of daily driver skills like these:

my-github is what needs my attention across GitHub: open PRs, review requests, assigned issues, recent merges.

andy-prs is every PR I opened, with its size, the issues it closes, the inbox report it came from, and its checks.

andy-issues is every issue I filed, mapped to the inbox report that picked it up and the PR that came out of it, so I can see which of my specs turned into code.

andy-approvals is the bot-authored PRs I approved or sent 
/trunk merge on, and whether the bot has pushed since, because approving an agent's PR and then losing track of it is a real failure mode.
A scout called 
signals-scout-andy-github runs the GitHub one every hour and keeps a single living report current in my inbox, so most mornings the answer is already waiting for me. A generic version, 
my-inbox, is in the community store.
5. Skills as a handover to humans
Before I went on holiday recently, I posted a state-of-the-world message to my team's Slack channel. It was long. It had a section on current state, a section on operational stuff, and a section on where to dig when something breaks.
Almost every bullet was a link to a skill.
Every bullet was a skill, so a teammate or their agent can pick it up:

scouts-dogfooding for the project log and open issues.

scouts-debugging for symptom-driven runbooks, including a playbook for digging into one team's experience.

scouts-dashboard for the dashboard I look at.

signals-alerts for what pages us. And the line I'm least sorry about: "if you have complex questions and analysis, say 'use the signals-dwh skill in PostHog MCP to help here'."
This is the bit I think people miss about a shared skills store: the handover doesn't go to a human who then has to load it into their own agent. It goes to the human and their agent at the same time, because the skill already lives where both of them can read it.
6. Skills that run themselves
Every scout in PostHog is a skill. Same format, same store, same version history. The only difference is a schedule and a harness that runs it. Which means when I've built a skill for how I do a job, turning it into a job that does itself is a small step, not a new project.

signals-scout-agent-feedback watches what agents complain about in our MCP, 
signals-scout-self-driving-logs watches our production logs, and 
signals-scout-canonical-drift checks the canonical scout fleet against the current harness once a week for any drift and inconsistencies as code evolves.
A few are about skills themselves. 
signals-scout-skills-best-practices checks recently-changed skills in our repo against the Agent Skills spec. 
signals-scout-skills-maintenance catches merged PRs that make an in-repo skill stale. Both lean on 
skills-best-practices, which gets its own section below.
Yes, I have skills that maintain skills. I did warn you.
7. Skills as a place to think
I even used a skill to write this blog. The 
andy-blogs skill has one file per post with the argument, sources, a dated log of every decision, a list of what I cut for being too sensitive, and the open TODOs. 
When I start a new session on the post, the agent already knows which branch the draft is on, which numbers it still has to re-check, and which Slack screenshot I already rejected (it was about scouts, not skills). It's well past 20 versions by now, and this paragraph is in its changelog. It helps with all the annoying stuff about writing blog posts like adding the screenshots. And I also use it to tell the agent how I write blog posts: I need to fire up VS Code to eyeball every diff before we commit, as agents are too eager to add stuff I don't want in the final post.
This isn't just a set of instructions. The skill is a document I'm iterating on with an agent, over weeks, across surfaces. A skill turned out to be a better home for that than a Google Doc, because the agent can read it, edit it with the smallest possible change, and every edit is a version I can diff.
Why the store, and not a folder of Markdown files
You could do all of this with a local 
.claude/skills/ or 
.agents/skills/ folder, but that's just crazy. Vibing your own plumbing and CI to get your skills to every agent is also totally possible but crazy. Using a skill store gives you benefits like:
It's on every surface. The same skill loads in Claude Code on my laptop, in a cloud task, in Slack, in Codex, in Cursor, and in PostHog AI.
Agents can write to it. The 
skill-update tool takes incremental 
edits and 
file_edits with a 
base_version check, so two sessions can maintain the same skill without clobbering each other.
It's versioned. 433 versions of 
self-driving-work means 433 diffs I can read when something looks off. A file on disk gives me one, unless I remember to commit it.
It's shared. A teammate, or their agent, or a scout, reads the same thing I do.
Progressive disclosure is built in. 
skill-list returns names and descriptions. 
skill-get returns the body and a file manifest. 
skill-file-get pulls one file.
It's not just me, either. Here's every skill created in our internal project since late April:
If you're already using the PostHog MCP, you have this today. Install the PostHog AI plugin and your agent already knows the 
skills-store skill. I keep a tiny local bridge called 
/phs that just loads it; the docs show how.
The skill that stops skills slop
There's a catch with all of this. Leave an agent to maintain a skill and it will grow it: a paragraph every session, a changelog line for every fix, until loading the skill costs more than it saves. A mono-skill of slop.
So I wrote 
skills-best-practices. I tell the agent to use it to clean up if needed and also, when I'm making a new project tracker type skill, I tell the agent to follow it. It's in the community store if you want it. The short version:
Give every skill a convention. Tell the agent exactly where an issue, a handover, or an investigation goes. If you don't, it makes something up, and it's different every time.
Keep the body small. About one screen: what this is, the gotchas, and a map of the files. Detail goes in the files.
Stop things growing forever. The changelog keeps 14 days. The handover gets overwritten, not appended to.
Link, don't copy. One skill per area, with links to its siblings.
Dogfood them. Use the skill for its actual job, notice where the agent stumbled, and fix the skill in the same session.
Try it
Read the skills docs and connect the PostHog MCP to whatever agent you use.
Then just ask your agent about the PostHog skills store. With the PostHog AI plugin installed, it already has the 
skills-store skill and knows how to list, load, and edit your skills.
Install 
project-template from the community store for one area of work you're tired of re-explaining to your agent.
Install 
skills-best-practices next to it, and tell your agent to load it before it creates or edits any skill.
When you have a skill for how you do a job, turn it into a scout and let it do the job for you.
And if you build a skill for something in your life that has no business being a skill, tell me. I have a hedgehog joke scout. I'm not going to judge.PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

How we use Logs at PostHog
Sara Miteva
Jan 23, 2026
Logs
If there’s something we do a lot here at PostHog (well, there’s many things but this one is top three), it’s dogfooding our own product. 
This is a crucial part of how we build better products. We're building tools for engineers, so having our own engineers using them helps us get feedback, feature requests, and even haikus.
Our team loves using Logs to debug PostHog. Here's the most important things they've learned about doing this effectively so far.
When “everything looks fine” isn’t true
For Sven LangeSven Lange, Platform Engineer in the Infrastructure Team, opening Logs usually means something already feels off. It might start with an alert, a bug report, or a suspicious anomaly. Sometimes, that means sanity-checking reports of things like SQL injection attempts and confirming there was no real impact.
One case stood out: repeated out-of-memory crashes on a node, with no obvious explanation. Sven opened Logs, filtered down to everything running on that node, and then started ruling things out. Normal-looking logs went first, then more normal-looking logs, until only something odd remained - gzipped noise showing up where it really shouldn’t.
That “noise” turned out to be an application logging huge compressed payloads. Our previous internal log pipeline dutifully tried to read all of it, but the logs were far too large and it kept crashing, sometimes taking other applications with it.
This was exactly the kind of problem the previous logging setup was good at hiding. That system discarded the problematic data, so everything looked mostly fine… apart for the unexplained crashes.
This wasn’t just a one-off investigation. Sven flagged this pattern to the team as a logging failure, not an infrastructure one – the system was hiding exactly the data you’d want when something goes wrong. That kic ked off a round of changes around how large payloads are handled, surfaced, and filtered in Logs.
Today, that same investigation usually starts by carving things down instead of staring at a wall of output. Include and exclude filters came directly out of these cases – the need to rule things out quickly without guessing. Tracking slow HTTP requests, for example, is as simple as filtering for requests over 600 ms and seeing the results update immediately.
Sven still checks Grafana/Loki when he needs older history, but for day-to-day investigations PostHog Logs has become the default. It’s become the default for day-to-day investigations, especially when the problem isn’t obvious yet.
Logs, but with the full picture
Rory ShanksRory Shanks and his team used to query built-in ClickHouse tables directly to inspect logs. It worked, but it wasn’t something you’d reach for when an issue was unfolding and you needed answers quickly. Until we built PostHog Logs.
Their setup now is intentionally simple. ClickHouse runs on EC2 as a 
systemd service. 
systemd writes logs to journald, Vector reads from 
journald, and sends everything to PostHog via OpenTelemetry. As a bonus, this doesn’t just include ClickHouse logs; it brings in system logs too.
Configuration is minimal, maintenance is basically zero, and anything that supports OTel “just works.”
Most of Rory’s questions are straightforward but time-sensitive:
When did this error start?
How widespread is it?
Can I quickly share this log with someone else?
The signals were technically available before, but Logs makes it much faster to see patterns, understand impact, and collaborate. Errors are easier to scope, links are easy to share, and everything loads fast, noticeably lighter than setups they’d used before, especially when all they needed was to understand scope and timing.
Debugging without the tab circus
Jon McCallumJon McCallum, Product Engineer in the Logs team, spends a lot of time inside Logs. Which actually makes total sense, because he’s one of the people working on it.
Jon rarely starts by staring at log lines and hoping for enlightenment (at least he says so). Instead, he narrows the blast radius first, a specific surface, service, or severity, until the noise drops enough for a pattern to show itself. As he tweaks the filters, the sparkline responds instantly, which is usually faster than his own intuition and much more honest.
Once something stands out, he digs into the details. Because logs are ingested as structured data, whether they come from OpenTelemetry or PostHog’s own SDKs, the metadata isn’t just there for reference. A trace ID or request ID becomes the fastest way to reframe the investigation. 
If he needs a quick reality check, Jon lets PostHog explain what the error is trying (and failing) to do, in human language. And when things are actively on fire, Live Tail is there to stream logs in real time. He says: 
The real superpower is how this connects to the front end, because we capture browser logs via PostHog JS. They’re automatically linked to the session and the user IDs. I can search for a front-end exception and jump directly into the session replay to watch the exact moment the bug happened.
This means that logs are now part of the same space as replays, errors, and analytics, which removes a lot of back-and-forth and makes debugging feel noticeably quicker.
Why you should try PostHog Logs too
Across teams, Logs tends to show up at the same moment, when something feels off and you want to confirm or rule it out quickly.
We keep using Logs because it’s shaped by the same problems we run into while building PostHog. When it gets in the way, it gets changed. When it works, it becomes part of the routine.
Try it out and start debugging where your data already is.PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

How startup secondaries actually work
Charles Cook
Feb 03, 2026
Guides, 
Explainers, 
Culture, 
People
Secondaries - so hot right now. For those not in the loop, a secondary stock sale or ‘secondary’ is where existing stockholders of a private company sell their stock to someone else. This is great for founders and employees - and early investors! - because they can realize some value in their stock without having to wait for some mythical IPO or (gasp) acquisition to happen. 
We’ve done two rounds of secondary sales at PostHog as part of our Series C and D, and we learned a lot of important details about how this stuff actually works. However, nobody is writing about this in any detail. Today I’m sharing those details with you. 
This guide is mainly written for founders and employees at US-based startups, so I’m going to assume you already understand what things like stocks, options and strike prices are. If you don’t, this primer may help. And it goes without saying, this post is 1000% not legal advice!
Why should I care?
The age of "get to $100m ARR and IPO at a $5bn valuation" is very much over. The emerging trend is now for the most successful startups to get very large while staying private - this allows them to keep control and not have to deal with things like public reporting requirements and stock prices. OpenAI and Stripe are two well-known examples, but even relatively smaller companies like Notion and ElevenLabs are doing it. And of course, PostHog. 
As startups stay private for longer, more investor money is flooding into secondaries - it’s a virtuous cycle. This is great for founders - they can now unlock liquidity for early employees so they don’t have to leave once their options have vested, while not feeling as much short-medium term pressure to realize a traditional exit. Instead, founders can focus on building the largest possible company while maximizing control. 
How are secondaries priced?
When investors buy stock in a primary financing (like investing in a startup's Series B), most of the time they are buying preferred stock. This means that a new type of stock is being created for that particular round and it comes with extra rights. However, the stock that founders and employees sell in a secondary are ordinary stock, which don’t come with these rights, and are just transferred to the investor - no new stock is created. 
These are the ways to deal with this mismatch when you do a round of funding with secondaries:
Investors buy and hold ordinary stock, paying the preferred price. This is the best move, but you need to be in a strong position with an oversubscribed round to pull this off. 
The cleanest way to do this is to have investors who are only buying secondary, rather than splitting primary and secondary across everyone. 

Investors buy and hold ordinary stock, but at a discount to the preferred price - the market standard is usually 20%. 

Investors buy ordinary stock at no discount, and that stock then convert to preferred afterwards. This can be a win-win BUT be careful of these gotchas: 
Something called QSBS comes into play - ask your lawyer. This is a very technical piece of tax law that your investors will really, really care about. 
You will increase your pref stack - more investors at the front of the queue to get paid out in a future liquidity event. 
If you have an EMI plan in the UK, timing and order here is really important - ask a UK lawyer or you risk tanking your entire EMI scheme. 
This is all assuming that you are doing primary and secondary financing at the same time - later on I’ll talk about why you might want to split them. 
How to offer secondaries to employees
This is the fun part. It’s also the bit that caused us the most angst. “Who do we let sell? How much can they sell? How long should they have been here? Do we set a $ cap? Will the team become demotivated if they sell too much? Will they not care if they sell too little?”
The most important thing is to have a basic set of rules you apply, so that you are taking the judgement out of it. These are the rules we settled on - feel free to copy them or modify to create your own:

Only open to all current employees. This was part admin, part fairness. On the admin side, you will be chasing your team a lot to hear what they want to do, sign documents, reply to boring questions about admin, etc. This is wayyy easier if they still work at the company. We also wanted to reward people who had stuck around at PostHog, as we’re still a relatively young company. 

Employees can sell up to 20% of their vested stock. 20% felt like a reasonable number - enough to make a difference in your life, but not enough to retire. Vested meant that only folks who had been with us > 1 year could sell stock (because of our 1-year vesting cliff), which again seemed fair. 
If you are the lucky person responsible for running this process internally, some other important things to consider. This is all stuff your lawyers are experts on, so talk to them:

There is a huge difference in the amount of (paper)work when fewer than 10 people sell stock vs more than 10. This figure includes your founders, if they are participating. 
Fewer than 10 people selling? You can just do this directly through your lawyers, it’s extra paperwork but it’s pretty straightforward. This is what we did the first time. 
More than 10 people selling? You are now doing an SEC-regulated tender offer, and will need to use a platform like Carta to manage the sale. This adds about 4 weeks to the process because you need to have the tender open for a minimum period, and Carta will charge a % of the proceeds as their fee (try to get buyers to pay for this or at least split the cost between buyers and sellers.) 

There are a few different ways the mechanics of exercising the stock options works. 
If your employees hold ISOs, they should exercise the options first themselves, i.e. they wire your company money, and then sell. This is better tax-wise for the employee. 
If they hold ISOs but can’t afford to exercise, then they should do cashless exercise, where the amount the employee pays to exercise is just deducted from the proceeds you send them, i.e. they don’t send any money. 

We had employees transacting directly with investors in the paperwork - your lawyers will handle all this. 
An alternative is to have your company buy all the stock from employees and then transact with investors - again your lawyers will advise mechanically what makes the most sense. 
The bit that no one tells you? Be prepared to spend half your time managing internal comms. Most of your team will have no idea how this stuff works. You will have to answer what you think are extremely basic questions, and have to chase a million times for bank details, addresses, signatures, etc. Be patient!
 If you are letting > 10 people sell, I strongly recommend you keep your primary and secondary financing rounds completely separate. It will slow down and complicate your primary financing round otherwise. 
Employees, this bit is for you
You may have read all of the above and thought "wow everyone is doing secondaries." The reality is they are still extremely rare, though growing in popularity! However, these are a few things you might want to consider up front:

Tax tax tax tax. If you work somewhere where a secondary is on the horizon, get a tax accountant lined up now. It will be 4x more stressful if you’re trying to do this at the same time as all the other paperwork. 

In the US and some other countries, early exercise can have tax benefits - google "83(b)" and then please talk to an accountant. 

If you work for a US startup but live outside the US, get an account set up that can receive USD like Wise or similar and then transfer out from there. Do not just have the money wired straight to your local currency account. For our non-US employees, this took 10min and literally saved them $000s. 
Finally, if you are interviewing for jobs and asking good questions, secondary strategy is probably more important than exit strategy in 2026. It is probably more useful to ask about how they think about secondaries and control more generally than "so, when’s that IPO happening?"

How to become a technical CSM (without an engineering background)ProductsPricingDocsCommunityCompanyMoreGet started – free

BlogCopy page
I became a technical CSM with ZERO training. You can too.
Ella Cullen
Sep 29, 2026
Inside PostHog
I’m Ella, I’m a technical customer success manager (CSM) at PostHog. I’m not an engineer. I did seven years in sales before moving into customer success, and I've been in customer success for about four and a half years now.
I have no computer science degree, and before joining PostHog I'd never shipped production code that a real team depends on. So, if you think you've missed the boat on becoming technical because you didn't come via an engineering degree or background, you haven’t.
Becoming "technical" in sales, account management, or success doesn't require attending a course or a bootcamp. It requires habits. 
When a customer asks something technical, try to answer it yourself before forwarding it to an engineer. This isn’t the norm in most customer success roles, because it’s riskier and takes longer, but it’s the habit that turned me into a genuinely technical CSM. 
That’s the TL;DR, for the long version, keep reading.
1. Work on a technical product (in a non-technical role)
This was the most impactful move I made. If you're coming from a non-technical background, walking straight into a technical CS role is hard, especially from sales. This gives you a much better start towards a deeper technical understanding.
For me, the way in was data. My first CS role was helping customers with a semantic layer, and most of the teams we worked with had never heard of one, let alone built with one. I had to be able to explain it to our customers, first at a high level (why semantic layers are important) and then progressively in more depth as our customers became more familiar with this approach.
The buyers were also highly technical – i.e. data teams, engineering managers, frontend and backend teams were involved. When your main point of contact with a customer is an engineer, you have to learn how the technical pieces fit together if you want to have any credibility.
2. Join a lean team makes you figure it out
The other thing that made me technical was not having anyone to fall back on. We were a small team, so no free engineer was sitting around waiting for my questions. It was faster to investigate questions and issues for myself, which also meant I learned faster as well.
When you’re a small team, you naturally want to limit how many questions you’re firing to the engineers. They are a precious resource, so you want them to see you as a good partner for them, as well as your customers.
In my experience, when engineers see you’re trying to get a handle on the technical stuff and answer questions for yourself, they really like that and are much more likely to jump in when you do need them. They trust you’re coming to them having already made some headway on the issue.
If you're on a big team with plenty of engineering support, you have to create this constraint for yourself. Before you escalate something, ask whether you could just work it out. Even if you can’t solve the whole thing yourself, digging into it means you’ll actually understand the solution when you do get it, rather than just applying a fix you don’t understand.
3. AI makes this easier than ever
So, not an original hot take, but it's important to call out, because 1) it's true and 2) most people are doing it wrong. I'm vibe coding, not hand-writing React, but being willing to vibe code at all already puts you a few steps ahead of most people in this job.
The key is to make sure you’re building something you actually use: vibe coding a little page that solves one problem and then never touching it again won’t teach you much, and this is what most folks are using AI for today.
Instead, you should build something end to end that solves a real problem you have, and then use it day after day. In my previous role, I built our whole customer success platform myself, because we didn't want to buy a tool and I wanted something that fit the systems we already had.
What’s important about what you build is that when you’re using something regularly, it will definitely break. And when it does, you have to work out why, and that's when the real learning happens. My troubleshooting was Claude + curiosity + slowly learning where to look when things went wrong. It helped that I was already digging around in the browser console with customers day to day, so I had a feel for where things tend to break.
4. Become a jack of all trades, not a master
People assume technical CSM means you need to be a data whiz, have hand-coded an app in React, and understand distributed systems. You don't.
If you are a master in a particular area, that will absolutely help. Your fellow CSMs and customers will likely be very grateful for your expertise! But what the job actually needs is:
A solid base
The ability to adapt when a customer throws something unfamiliar at you
Enough curiosity to keep learning and to care what your customers are doing
Your job is to understand how the pieces fit together and be an expert on how they can get the most value from your platform (which, yes, if you're lucky and you work somewhere with high trust, can also mean shipping bug fixes and features to production).
If the above sounds like you – curious, stubborn about working things out, and excited about technical concepts – technical customer success might suit you. Oh and PostHog is hiring for this exact role right now in both NA and EU. Wow, what a crazy coincidence.PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

How to benchmark AI agents at scale against real dataProductsPricingDocsCommunityCompanyMoreGet started – free

Do you even benchmark? How we evaluate agents at scale (with real examples)
Alex Lebedev
Oct 28, 2026
Inside PostHog, 
Engineering, 
AI, 
AI observability
We spend 2 trillion+ LLM tokens per month, with the lion's share going to running agents. We know what they do and how good they are most of the time, but we spend way too much money on them to trust their output based on vibes alone.
That's why we use benchmarks. 
Labs like Anthropic and OpenAI use them to measure, compare, and market new models on release, like the popular SWE-bench, which is designed to evaluate model performance on general coding tasks.
But benchmarks aren't just for frontier labs. They're useful for anyone who wants to understand how well a model, harness, or skill works in their given stack. For example, you might run three different models with the same code review prompt on the same PR to choose the best one based on how many known bugs they catch, how long they take, and what they cost.
The idea is similar to running controlled experiments, but in reality, benchmarking is never that easy. Evaluation is often subjective, behavior is unpredictable, and – perhaps most painful of all – agents love to cheat. They'll search for leaked context, memory, and database query logs to pass benchmark tests with as little work as possible.
In this post, I'll explain how we benchmark our agents at PostHog, what we learned, and where we messed up (so you don't have to) – all with links to real PRs.
A. Define the answer key
If a benchmark is like a standardized test, the first thing you need is an answer key: the list of correct answers you grade your against.
This is the hardest part, in my opinion. If you ask an LLM judge whether an agent's output is "helpful", you'll get polite, useless praise. Especially if the same model generated it.
For a benchmark to actually be useful, the criteria for what's "good" or not needs to match the complexity they will encounter on the job. Simple yes/no sanity checks won't cut it since agentic tasks are typically more complicated than that. 
Here are the three approaches we tried in increasing order of difficulty and complexity.
Level 1: A list of potential bugs from one PR
Our first approach was to take a task with clear answers and check which agents succeed, versus which ones fail. Each agent had three variables: the model, effort level, and harness.
We did this to evaluate our internal code review agent called ReviewHog, which covers a significant part of PostHog PRs. ReviewHog needs to stay up to date for the best results, so we needed a base benchmark to check against when we change models or prompts.
The best solution we came up with initially was surprisingly effective and simple:
First, we took one large PR.
Then, we made a "frozen copy" of it.
Humans reviewed the frozen PR manually.
We then asked several review agents to review it.
This produced a pretty exhaustive list of potential bugs from every possible angle.

So if there were 13 issues worth checking for (structure, performance, security, etc.), we could measure the models on a 0/13 scale, plus compare how much time and money each one cost. Here's an example report of us testing ReviewHog this way with GLM 5.3 Flash.
It worked (and still works) well, but it has an obvious limitation: the answer key is based on one single PR for one single change in one single repo. No matter how large that PR is, this approach would never be able to cover all the other types of bugs that could happen in all of our repos.
Level 2: A larger, golden set from multiple PRs
The second approach we used for benchmarking ReviewHog involved the same method, but across a larger percentage of real cases and with more varied examples.
Getting more PRs was easy; our team produces 10K PRs a month.
But then we had an idea. What if instead of looking for synthetic bugs, we created an answer key by searching for real bugs that actually happened? It would be even better if those bugs caused real messes, like proper incidents, since those are exactly the types of things we want these code review agents to prevent.
So that's what we did.

We looked through old PostHog tickets to create a golden set of 33 actual incidents, the PRs that caused them, descriptions of the problem, and the PR that fixed the incident. We analyzed each of them with ReviewHog and other bots to compare their performance, and the results were pretty good:
ReviewHog found the incident-causing bugs in 62% of the cases
In 47% of the cases, ReviewHog was the only bot that discovered those bugs, while other bots missed them
In 9% of the cases, ReviewHog skipped the bug because another bot raised it before ReviewHog started the review, so ReviewHog marked it as "already known"
In 6% of cases, the bugs were found by other bots, while ReviewHog didn't find them

The best combination we got at the time was with 
GPT Sol 5.6 at 
xhigh for bug search, and 
Claude Opus 5 at 
xhigh for bug validation, both using 
pi as the harness. You can check out our repo for the full experiment results. 1
Remember, these benchmarks are specific to our use cases. Just because this combination of model, harness, and effort worked well for ReviewHog doesn't mean it will be the optimal choice for another codebase or task. That's the whole point of creating specific benchmarks for your specific stack and tasks.
Overall, there were still some downsides of this "larger golden set" method, but it was still acceptable:

For 33 incidents, we had to resurrect the 33 PRs that caused them and then analyze the 33 PRs that fixed them. This created lots of noise and triggered false alarms from our GitHub bots.

We didn't re-add the bugs to the codebase. That would be bad. Instead, we kept them as isolated PRs by properly locking the branch for the agent.

With open-source repos like ours, an agent with web access can still look up the public repo, merged PRs, and cheat. (More on this later.)
That said – and you probably thought about this, too – this only works because code review tasks are fairly deterministic and relatively easier to grade. The next problem we hit was how to grade agents for more abstract and subjective tasks.
Level 3: Targeted, contextual rubrics
Benchmarking gets a lot more complicated when you're trying to evaluate agents that can technically do anything.
A great example is Scouts, our implementation of scheduled custom agents that let you research anything. That could range from your Product Analytics anomalies in PostHog, to mentions of your brand in social media, to recurring themes in your internal Slack. These tasks are as open-ended as it gets.
Much like how an A-B-C-D format answer key makes sense for grading multi-select quizzes but not for grading an essay, we needed to come up with a different way to evaluate scouts on open-ended tasks.
The obvious answer was rubrics – scoring and evaluation guides that describe the ideal answer, rather than containing the answer itself. But feneric rubrics like "Rate accuracy from 1 to 5" fall apart immediately when evaluating agents. They do a great job of measuring how confident and fluent the model sounds, not whether it did useful work.
Our solution was to build a rubric generator that creates guidelines based on the agent's context. We do this in two steps for scouts.
First, all scouts follow the same procedures, even if they work across wildly different domains. So we have one set of static rubrics shared across all scouts that checks whether the scout produced a report covering what it found, how actionable the findings are, and what to do next. 
We then also generate rubrics tailored to that specific scout based on context that was been provided to the scout so far, such as:
The area it covers (e.g. a feature, an external source, etc.)
Skills and instructions it needs to follow during runs
Previous runs (e.g. tools it used, reports it generated)
For example, to benchmark a scout analyzing the stability of the Session Replay player, we don't just check its report formatting. We also grade whether it spotted actual playback failure symptoms, queried data correctly, and whether the bug it flagged actually affected real users – criteria specific to Session Replay.

With these rubrics in place, we could reliably track scout success rates across different agent configurations. The v1 of this tailored rubric system allowed us to test against:
What we testQuestion
ModelsDo scouts work better with the new model, or the old one?
Thinking effortDo scouts actually need to think at xhigh levels, if medium does it just fine with 30% fewer tokens?
Prompt changesIf we create 5 different versions of the skill, which version works best for each task?
The result is a report with a close-to-clear answer. It's not 100% deterministic, but it's way better than just "vibes".
Here's an example of a report I ran while writing this blog to check whether Sol or Luna performs better for one of our scouts. The results suggest we should stick with Sol for this one; Luna could do a better job on plenty of other tasks, but to know that, you need something measurable.

If you want to see how our rubric generator and ranking work under the hood, check out our code.
So all of those three approaches were just the first step of developing an answer key or grading system for the agents. After defining what's "good", we need to make these tests work and stay objective at scale.
B. Isolate benchmark runs
The surprisingly nasty problem we learned is that when you benchmark multiple models against real data, they'll quickly do everything they can to learn about and piggyback off of each other. They might source answers from LLM traces, DB queries, or any other logs the agentic run generates.
Here's an example of a data-anomalies scout being benchmarked. Run B4 investigated an anomaly and saved a memory at 15:18:08. When Run B12 ran later in the same workspace, it picked up that memory at 15:18:54 and used it instead of doing the work itself:

This defeats the purpose of benchmarking since the results aren't reflecting the actual agent's performance. 
With multi-step agents that simulate human-agent conversation, state leaks into places that normal test runners don't even check. This next section is about the three approaches we tried to isolate runs to preserve benchmark integrity.
Level 1: Parallel runs with no shared state
This approach is only valid if your agents don't generate meaningful artifacts (like traces, memory files, and logs) beyond the output that gets graded. Potential examples include simple classifiers or summarizers. 
In these cases, you could run multiple variants at the same time; no shared state means no contamination. But in most cases (at least, for us at PostHog), our agents are complex and have many potential places to leak information, such as through observability tools or error logs.
So let's go back to the B4 and B12 example above to explain the failure modes. 
Failure mode #1 is when cheating makes an agent appear better than it actually is. An agent using a faster but lighter model like Luna could easily just read and copy notes from an agent running on Opus.
Failure mode #2 is when shared state leads smarter models to make decisions that make them seem worse than they are, such as skipping a task because it sees that an another agent already completed. One time, during a benchmark run, Run B2 looked at candidate anomalies, saw that an earlier run had already covered the target bug, and skipped that candidate entirely:

In this case, a clever model would get a surprisingly low grade for not finding a basic issue, or you would need to prepare your judges for similar cases, which would affect the benchmarking results anyway.
So, unless the agents you're evaluating don't produce any artifacts, you need a way to make each run invisible to the others.
Level 2: Sequential runs with state cleanup
A simple approach to isolate the runs is to just run them sequentially with cleanup between each run – i.e. run a trial, record the output, reset the agent's context, and then start the next run

This doesn't mean you can only run one agent – the chain could include hundreds of agents running in sequence, or in parallel if they are all part of the same task. This is what we did for the initial ReviewHog benchmarks against a single frozen PR (Step 1, Option A).
The downsides of this are clear: you need to clean up the DB and logs after each run, and it's obviously slow, so testing different combinations of agents/efforts/skills takes a long time.
Level 3: Parallel runs with total isolation
Most of us don't have unlimited time and patience to do sequential runs. The good news is that there is a way to get clean benchmarks in parallel. The bad news is that it's not simple – every trial needs complete isolation across everything the agent can touch:
Identical starting context across all runs
Private writable state (scratchpads, memory, vector stores, and DBs)
Separate evaluation so scoring happens independently
DB state isn't the only leak. If your agent has tools to query ClickHouse, PostHog, logs, and so on, an earlier benchmark run leaves traces in those sources. A subsequent run can find those error spikes or query histories and use them as clues. True isolation means isolating telemetry and log scopes too.

There's also a risk of over-isolating. If the benchmarking agent doesn't have as many tools as the real agent, it can get confused and skew the results unrealistically.
Here's an example of one of the first dry-runs we tested. It differs from the previous two traces; it wasn't cheating, just following instructions a bit too literally and promised not to write any inbox reports:

Because the dry-run agent doesn't execute all the steps an actual run would (creating new reports, editing data, and so on), it left blind spots we couldn't test. This was acceptable for our case with scouts, since we care more about how they retrieve information than how they store it.
If these types of blind spots are a blocker for your agent and critical to your evaluation, the next best option is to create truly isolated environments where agents can access all tools, but this requires freezing state.
C. Freeze the environment (a.k.a., offline evals)
You can technically run hundreds of isolated agents with full tool access against the production database pretty reliably. But this will also interfere with the benchmark because it means state and data is not controlled between runs. You can't compare between them equally since it raises the question: "did this agent's score improve because of the variables we're testing, or because something in the data changed?"
We solved this by moving benchmarks from a "production environment that changes all the time" to a "production environment with the same starting state" – i.e. frozen environments. To do this, we had to replicate or simulate our app, inject real (or real-enough) data, and make the agent believe it's a real thing. We call these offline benchmarks.
That's a lot. So why bother?

Since frozen environments have a fixed starting point, you can easily reset them after every run, solving problems with data leaks. In our case, we run a copy of PostHog inside VMs, delete the VM after each benchmark, and spawn a new one.

It also means that the agent is actually allowed to change the state, write, create, delete, etc. as we test the task end to end, leaving fewer blind spots.

As a bonus, because the data stays fixed, the benchmark you did for model X a month or two ago will still be comparable to the benchmark for model Y you did today.
I'm using the word "offline" loosely here since the agents will still need connectivity to call AI endpoints and such. The point is that state is frozen, and can be reset at any time.
We went through three stages to get this working.
Level 1: Mocked MCP replies
The first thing we tried was to create mock MCP calls of the agent, so when agent thinks it's querying the DB, it's actually just getting a pre-stored answer to what it asked for before in prod. For example, what query it ran with 
execute_query(sql) and what slice of the DB it returned:

This sounds straightforward and worked well for basic tech demos, like returning static JSON to SQL queries, but it failed miserably on any meaningful production-like work. 
This is because agents aren't deterministic; the query from Run 1 doesn't guarantee that Run 2 will run the same one. And since we had to mock MCP replies in advance, if the agent asks something different or new compared to the runs from prod we recorded, we couldn't always provide a reasonable answer.
It's not a big surprise, but it would still be cool if it worked out-of-the-box. Still, the case isn't that desperate, and we tried a couple of tweaks.
Level 2: Trajectory-based mocked MCP replies
The logical next step was to build mock database on ~50 runs instead of just a single run. In this version, we based the mock replies on every trajectory the agent picked (i.e., the complete, ordered sequence of steps, reasoning, tool calls, and observations it produced from start to finish).
This seemed promising for a while. Thanks to the trajectory-based approach, we were able to guess most of the queries well at first. But eventually in the run, some drift would happen here and there due to nondeterminism, and then an outlier query would return nothing. The agent then gets confused, the run fails, etc. 
For how much effort this approach takes, it's not really worth it if you already have access to real data. If you do choose this route, I'd suggest adding synthetic (or real) data a bit before and/or after every query so that a 24h query still returns true data if the call is skewed a bit.
For us, since most of our benchmarking needs at PostHog were for internal tasks, we do have access to lots of real data, so we decided to stop messing with mocked MCP replies and go with an approach more grounded in real data.
Level 3: Restored real-data slices
The solution that actually worked for us was to spin up an isolated PostHog sandbox seeded with a restored, real-world data slice.
On the surface, the idea was simple: query a couple of DB tables (Postgres, ClickHouse), store them as Parquet files in S3, and then restore them in the VM with a local PostHog instance to make it look like the real deal. The bonus: data never leaves PostHog infra.

The first problem we encountered was with timestamps. If an agent in a frozen environment asks for the last 24h of events, we'll have prepared enough data for it to work fine for today, or at least for a few hours. But if you run the test again tomorrow, the agent will fail because it's using real UTC time on static data. A query for September 17 won't return anything if the frozen environment only contains data from September 15-16. 
The solution was simple enough: every time we injected data, we'd correct it to match the frozen timeline by shifting it.
The second problem was less obvious. Even though we tried to make the data slices as realistic as possible, there were still certain types of data that we didn't want to replicate.
We wanted the slices to be as small as possible since the environments need to be easy to create and reset. We didn't expect the tasks to need all of the data anyway, but thanks to non-determinism, new models would still sometimes try to look into tables and data sources that we didn't slice. 
A common one we encountered was user tables, which we deliberately chose not to duplicate since they contain PII (Personally Identifiable Information). But an agent would sometimes decide it wanted to look inside those tables for seemingly unrelated tasks. It would then see that there weren't many users on its local instance, and immediately suspect something was strange.

On the other hand, it's also possible to overprepare the data. You could make it as realistic as possible on the MCP tools side, but if the rest of the data in the local instance doesn't match the scale, then the agent gets even more suspicious and starts thinking the data is synthetic.

Once the agent starts treating the investigation as a test, it starts behaving in strange ways like:
Stopping at a good-enough explanation instead of running extra queries to verify it.
Spending part of its budget investigating gaps or inconsistencies in the restored data instead of the actual task.
Returning more speculative findings that it would normally leave out.
Any of those behaviors can negatively affect your benchmark's integrity since they're not realistic. And, sadly, there's no silver bullet – you just have to run and tweak it over and over again until you stop seeing "the agent suspects something" traces anymore.
Conclusion
Building quality benchmarks sounds like a lot of work because it is, but it's entirely worth it. You'll end up with a solid system that will let you move faster in the long run, especially if you don't repeat the mistakes we made.
 Parts A and B are now part of PostHog and going through internal testing. We're still working on Part C, freezing environments, but wanted to share our learnings so far. 
If you take anything away from this blog, it's that agents will happily exploit whatever mess you leave behind and cheat. Watch for unexpected parameters, iterate a lot, and pay attention to traces. 
Vibes can still take you pretty far in the short run, especially for smaller and simpler use cases. But for anyone who wants to get serious about evaluating AI at scale – it's time to bench.
A big takeaway from this is to always use different model families for detection and validation. We got miserable results when we used either OpenAI or Anthropic models for both stages.↩PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

What is user segmentation? - PostHogProductsPricingDocsCommunityCompanyMoreGet started – free
